description: Whole modules, for questions a single declaration cannot ask: whether an expression the evaluator cannot fold is refused or aborts the build.

entries.label: a string method inside a runtime condition
entries.origin: issue #1265, the reported input

entries.label: an array method inside a runtime condition
entries.origin: issue #1265, the second reported input

entries.label: an unfoldable operand reached through a binding
entries.origin: issue #1265, the reporter's fuller module
entries.note: The reporter's fuller module, verbatim. `borderTop: none` declares nothing in either compiler: `property-specificity` rejects the shorthand and `propertyValidationMode: silent` drops it. The `display` rule and the surviving condition are what this entry is about.

entries.label: every shape of unfoldable call in a runtime condition
entries.origin: issue #1265, the shapes behind the reported one

entries.label: an unfoldable callback argument reached through a binding
entries.origin: issue #1265, found while pinning the shapes
entries.note: Acceptance divergent in this compiler's favour: upstream aborts with `Unsupported expression: ObjectPattern`, reaching the destructured parameter through the callback body and throwing from an evaluation allowed to fail. The same defect #1265 reports here. Written inline in the `sx` array instead of through `matches`, it compiles upstream too.

entries.label: a length read off a string, in every static position
entries.origin: issue #1265, found while comparing the reporter's output

entries.label: a length read off a string that is not ASCII
entries.origin: issue #1265, the convention a length has to be counted in

entries.label: a length read off an array
entries.origin: issue #1265, the same rule on the other receiver

entries.label: a length read off an array carrying a hole
entries.origin: issue #1265, found while deciding where the count is read from
entries.note: Acceptance divergent in this compiler's favour. A hole is a slot, so the language says two; upstream refuses the whole array with `Could not resolve the code being evaluated` rather than counting it.

entries.label: a length read off an array carrying a spread
entries.origin: issue #1265, found in code review of the length fold
entries.note: Both reject. A spread is one written element standing for however many the spread value holds, so neither the written count nor the evaluated one is the language's answer and both compilers refuse rather than fold a wrong number.

entries.label: property reads next to a length, including the one that still diverges
entries.origin: issue #1265, the reads that surround the one being fixed
entries.note: A property neither a string nor an array carries answers `undefined` in both compilers, so the `??` fallback folds identically. Kept as its own subject because it is the half of the member path that is parity and the indexed read below is the half that is not.

entries.label: an indexed read, the one member lookup that still diverges
entries.origin: issue #1265, the read that surrounds the one being fixed
entries.note: Acceptance divergent. Upstream folds `"abc"[0]` to `"a"` through the language; this compiler refuses. Refusing is deliberate: upstream folds `"\u{1F600}"[0]` to a lone surrogate, which no Rust `String` can carry, so folding an index needs a value type that carries WTF-8 through the whole pipeline.

entries.label: every property the specificity table refuses, beside one it does not
entries.origin: issue #1265, the shorthand rejection table
entries.note: All eighteen rejected names must declare nothing while `color` survives, so the verdict reads a real pair of declarations rather than an empty one. A regression that lets any shorthand through turns this structurally divergent.

entries.label: a `null` style value, in every position that can carry one
entries.origin: issue 10, the positions a `null` reaches
entries.note: Every entry must keep its property present and carrying `null`, which only the style-object half of the comparison can see -- an absent value emits no CSS either way. An array carrying only `null` is the one this compiler used to drop the key for, and `emptyArray` is the neighbouring case that legitimately has no key at all; the two must not collapse into one answer.

entries.label: a `null` on a shorthand, under the default resolution
entries.origin: issue 10, the shorthand positions a `null` reaches

entries.label: a boolean style value, where nothing validates it
entries.origin: issue 10, the calls with no value validator in front of them

entries.label: a `null` as the whole value of a condition key, which still diverges
entries.origin: issue 10, measured while settling what a `null` means
entries.note: Structurally divergent, deliberately. Upstream treats the condition key itself as a property name and emits a key hashed from `:hover` carrying `null`; this compiler emits nothing. Neither key can carry CSS, and neither can collide with a real declaration made under the same condition, so reproducing a property named after a pseudo-class would bake a defect in rather than fix one. Filed upstream instead.

entries.label: a boolean style value inside create, which both compilers refuse
entries.origin: issue 10, the other half of what a boolean means
entries.note: Expected `both reject`. It earns an entry because the answer used to depend on where the boolean was written -- refused directly, compiled and silently dropped under a condition -- and a corpus that only asks the position that already worked would not have caught that.

entries.label: a spread of a string literal in a fallback array
entries.origin: found while reviewing the panic/deopt split
entries.note: The shape that made the spread refusal necessary. This compiler folded it to `["ab"]` and shipped `color:ab`, where the language spreads two characters and upstream refuses. A wrong stylesheet, not a missing refusal, which is why it is held here rather than only in the Rust suite.

entries.label: a spread of a number in a fallback array
entries.origin: found while reviewing the panic/deopt split
entries.note: `[...1]` throws in the language. This compiler shipped `color:1`.

entries.label: a spread of a binding in a fallback array
entries.origin: found while reviewing the panic/deopt split
entries.note: Refused by both, but this compiler used to refuse it by the value rule and so reported a different sentence than upstream's `Unsupported expression: SpreadElement`.

entries.label: a spread of an operand the evaluator cannot resolve
entries.origin: found while reviewing the panic/deopt split
entries.note: Pins the order: upstream never evaluates a spread's operand, so the refusal names the spread and not the operand. This compiler reported `Unsupported expression: ArrayExpression` until the check moved ahead of the operand.

entries.label: a spread nested one array deep
entries.origin: found while reviewing the panic/deopt split
entries.note: Pins that an element's refusal is carried up rather than renamed after its container: this reported `Unsupported expression: ArrayExpression`, naming a node the author did not write.

entries.label: a spread argument to stylex.firstThatWorks
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Refused by both. Upstream answers `Unsupported expression: SpreadElement` for every spread, whatever the callee. This compiler reported `Function argument must be a static expression.`

entries.label: a spread argument to a Math method
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Refused by both. Upstream answers `Unsupported expression: SpreadElement` for every spread, whatever the callee. This compiler reported that the spread operator is not supported in this context.

entries.label: a spread argument to a string method
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Refused by both. Upstream answers `Unsupported expression: SpreadElement` for every spread, whatever the callee. This compiler reported `All arguments must be a string`.

entries.label: a spread argument to an array method
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Refused by both. Upstream answers `Unsupported expression: SpreadElement` for every spread, whatever the callee. This compiler reported `Unsupported expression: CallExpression`, naming the call rather than the spread.

entries.label: an object spread of a value with no own properties
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: `Object.assign({}, 1)` is `{}`, so spreading a primitive adds nothing and the object is built from the rest. This compiler refused the whole call instead, failing a build over an expression that means "add nothing".

entries.label: an object spread of a string
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: A string's own properties are its indices, so this declares `0` and `1`. This compiler refused it.

entries.label: an object spread of an array
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: An array's own properties are its indices, and each value keeps its type -- which is why these declare `1px` and `2px` rather than strings.

entries.label: an object spread of more than one key
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Pins the order the properties come out in. The merge assembled its result by pushing the old properties onto the new and reversing the whole thing, so every spread of more than one key emitted its rules back to front. One key is the common case and hid it.

entries.label: an object spread overriding an earlier key
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: A repeated key takes the later value and keeps the position the key first took, as `Object.assign` does.

entries.label: an object spread replacing a nested object
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: `Object.assign` is shallow, so the nested `color` is replaced rather than merged in. Nesting is most of what a style object is made of, so a deep merge here would quietly keep declarations the source had replaced.

entries.label: an object spread of an array carrying a hole
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Both refuse. This evaluator drops a hole before it becomes a value, so the keys after it would come out shifted -- `{ 0: 1 }` where the language says `{ 1: 1 }`. Upstream crashes outright on this input, so refusing it costs nothing.

entries.label: a regular expression in a style value
entries.origin: found while mirroring the spread refusal to upstream
entries.note: Upstream folds no `RegExpLiteral` in any position. This compiler folded one to itself and left the refusal to whichever downstream reader tripped over the value, which had no name for it -- the diagnostic came out as `1`. `String(/re/)` did not refuse at all: it wrote `color: / re /` into the stylesheet.

entries.label: an index key enumerated before a named one
entries.origin: found in review of the object-spread work
entries.note: An object enumerates every array-index key first in ascending numeric order, then every other key in insertion order -- and that is the order the declarations reach the stylesheet. This compiler used pure insertion order, so `color` came out before `0`.

entries.label: a non-canonical numeric key keeps its place
entries.origin: found in review of the object-spread work
entries.note: A key is an array index only in its canonical decimal spelling, so `'00'` is an ordinary string key and stays where it was written. Guards the ordering rule against over-reaching.

entries.label: a numeric key large enough to need exponent notation
entries.origin: found in review of the object-spread work
entries.note: A numeric key is spelled the way JavaScript spells the number: `1e+21`. This compiler formatted it with Rust's `f64` rendering and named the property `1000000000000000000000`, which changed both the declaration and its class name.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named theme import
entries.origin: issue #1266, the reported input
entries.note: The parameter and the import share a symbol and nothing else. Resolving an import by its name rather than its binding answered a confident theme reference for the parameter and aborted the build; the static prop beside it has to keep its theme reference at the same time, which is why this is a module and not a declaration.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing an aliased theme import
entries.origin: issue #1266, the aliased variant found while auditing the lookup
entries.note: Failed identically to the unaliased shape, and for the same reason: the local binding is what a reference resolves through, and `zi` is the local binding here.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter written before the static read
entries.origin: issue #1266, the prop-order variant
entries.note: Property order is irrelevant to the defect -- a dynamic style's body is evaluated whichever side of the static read it is written on. Recorded so a future evaluation-order change cannot make the fix order-dependent without saying so.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter whose import is read nowhere else
entries.origin: issue #1266, the shape that compiled before the fix
entries.note: This shape agreed twice over, and the first reason is gone. The type-stripping pass used to elide an import with no value reference before the StyleX pass, so the name match had nothing to match; a `.js` subject now keeps the specifier, so the declaration is there and the match runs. It still agrees, on the binding comparison alone -- which is what this row was kept for. The elision half is `modules-1266-param-shadows-a-named-import-referenced-nowhere-else`.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter whose import is read outside any create call
entries.origin: issue #1266, the isolation that pinned the mechanism
entries.note: Any value reference to the binding, anywhere in the module, kept the import declaration alive and made the name match fire. Reading it outside every `create()` call is the shape that rules out the evaluation cache as the cause.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter read at every depth of a condition tree
entries.origin: issue #1266, written to reach the recursive value walk
entries.note: The value walk recurses per condition key, so the shadowed reference is resolved once per leaf. A fix that only held at the top level of a style value would show here.

entries.label: two dynamic parameters shadowing two theme imports
entries.origin: issue #1266, written to reach more than one import declaration
entries.note: The lookup scans a flat list of declarations, so one shadowed binding must not decide the answer for another. Both parameters shadow, both static reads keep their theme reference.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a module-level const
entries.origin: issue #1266, the shape that already worked and says why
entries.note: A guard. The declaration lookup was already binding-aware, which is what made a shadowed `const` resolve correctly while a shadowed import did not -- the asymmetry that located the defect. It has to keep resolving that way.

entries.label: an unshadowed dynamic parameter beside a theme read
entries.origin: issue #1266, the control
entries.note: A guard: the same module with the parameter renamed. A fix that stopped resolving imports altogether would pass every shadowing case above and fail here.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter whose name is not ASCII
entries.origin: issue #1266, written to reach a non-ASCII binding name
entries.note: Bindings are compared as interned atoms, so a name outside ASCII is no different -- pinned because a comparison written over bytes or lowercased text would be.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter spelled with a unicode escape
entries.origin: issue #1266, written to reach an escaped binding name
entries.note: `\u007AIndex` is `zIndex`: the lexer folds the escape, so the parameter shadows the import exactly as the plain spelling does, and the body's `zIndex` is the parameter. Pinned because the escape is the one spelling where the source text and the binding name differ.

entries.label: a style value reading a const declared later in the module
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the one divergence that was wrong output
entries.note: Declarations are collected module-wide with no notion of position, so the initializer was reachable from above its own declaration and this compiled to `.x…{color:red}` -- CSS for a value the program does not hold yet. The reference implementation refuses it. Recorded as both rejecting so the refusal cannot quietly go away.

entries.label: a style value reading a const declared before it
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the guard on the position comparison
entries.note: The same pair in program order. Without it a comparison that refused every declared binding would read as a fix.

entries.label: a shorthand style value reading a const declared later
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, written to reach shorthand expansion
entries.note: A shorthand is expanded into synthesized longhands, and a synthesized node carries no authored position. The value they carry is the reference as authored, so the position survives the expansion and the refusal still lands -- as it does upstream.

entries.label: a style value reading a const initialized from itself
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the boundary case of the position comparison
entries.note: `const c = c` puts a reference inside the declarator it names, so it starts before that declarator ends and is early by the same comparison. Both compilers refuse it, and for that reason rather than for the cycle.

entries.label: a props call reading a theme binding declared after the component
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, found by a fixture that changed
entries.note: Styles written below the component that uses them is the ordinary shape, and a bare theme reference in a `props` call is early by the position comparison, so both compilers leave the call to the runtime. This compiler used to fold it to a class list instead, which is a divergence nothing was measuring.

entries.label: a props call reading a styles member declared after the component
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the asymmetry beside the entry above
entries.note: A member read of a later `create()` result still folds, in both compilers: the position comparison is reached by a bare reference, and a member access resolves through the namespace it names. The asymmetry is upstream's, and this records that it is matched rather than reasoned about.

entries.label: a theme import aliased to the name of a global the evaluator folds
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the one pair the step reorder is not inert on
entries.note: `NaN` is a legal binding name, so this is the only shape where an import specifier and one of the three folded globals name the same binding -- and the resolution chain asks about the import first, as the reference implementation does. Before the chain was ordered, the globals were asked about first and this folded to a literal `NaN`. Recorded because it is the single outcome the reorder changed, and it changed toward the reference implementation. Measured both ways: `acceptance divergent` at 0f9d2bcd2, `identical` once the chain is ordered.

entries.label: a member read off a default import of a theme file
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the default-import step of the resolution chain
entries.note: A theme file is read through its named exports, so a default binding names nothing either compiler can fold. Upstream refuses with `There was an error when attempting to evaluate the imported file.`; this compiler resolved the default specifier as a theme reference like any other and emitted `.x…{color:var(--xe7srj8)}` -- a variable the theme file does not define, which is `acceptance divergent`. Measured with no shadowing anywhere in the module, so the divergence is about the import specifier kind and nothing else. Both refuse once the step lands.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a default theme import, with the import read nowhere else
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the default-import step asked of a shadowing binding
entries.note: The refusal above is keyed to the binding, so a parameter that merely spells the import's name is not the import and still compiles to an inline style. This is the entry a regression from a binding match back to a name match would break -- it would resolve the parameter to the default specifier and refuse, where the entry above would keep reading `both reject` and say nothing.

entries.label: one import declaration carrying both a default and a named theme specifier
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the guard on the default-import step
entries.note: The chain asks which *specifier* binds the reference, not which declaration does, and one declaration can carry both kinds with opposite answers. Recorded so that refusing a default import cannot quietly start refusing the named specifier beside it.

entries.label: a default import of a module that is not a theme file, read as a style value
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the default-import step reached without a theme file
entries.note: Nothing about the refusal is specific to a theme file -- the step is reached before the import path is resolved at all, so the message no longer depends on where the file sits. Recorded because this compiler refused for the *path* before the step landed and refuses for the *specifier* now, and only measurement says whether that is the reason upstream gives.

entries.label: a call through a default import, as a style value
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the callee position of the default-import step
entries.note: The reference is the callee rather than the value, which reaches the chain by a different route. This is the shape `invalid_value_non_static_import_default` asserts, and its message changed with the step -- measured rather than reasoned about, because a message the reference implementation does not give is a divergence however right the refusal is.

entries.label: a dynamic style's parameter named `NaN`
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the globals step of the resolution chain
entries.note: `NaN` is an ordinary binding name, so a parameter can take it over -- and the resolution chain has to ask which of the two the reference in the body is. It asks about the binding, so the parameter refuses and the value falls through to the inline-style path a dynamic parameter is emitted through. Before the step asked, the global folded in and CSS generation rejected the static `NaN` with `Only static values are allowed inside of a create() call.`, which is `acceptance divergent`.

entries.label: a dynamic style's parameter named `Infinity`, and one named `undefined`
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the two names beside `NaN`
entries.note: The step answers for all three names alike. Kept beside the `NaN` entry rather than folded into it so a regression that reaches only one of the three still reports.

entries.label: a parameter named `NaN` read through arithmetic
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the refusal travelling out of an operand
entries.note: The refusal has to travel out of the arithmetic rather than being the value the property receives, which is a different path out of the evaluator than the bare reference above. Before the step asked, this folded to the literal `NaN` and emitted `width:NaNpx`, which upstream does not: `divergent`.

entries.label: a module-level `const` named `NaN`, read from a style value
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the globals step outside a dynamic style
entries.note: The step refuses for any binding, not only a parameter, and it refuses *instead of* reading the declarator's initializer -- a reference that names a binding never reaches the initializer step. Both compilers refuse, with the same text: `Referenced constant is not initialized.` Before the step asked, this compiler folded the initializer and emitted `width:5px` where upstream refused: `acceptance divergent`.

entries.label: the global `NaN` in a module where an unrelated scope binds the name
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the guard on the globals step
entries.note: The binding question is asked of the reference's full `Id`, so a binding of the same name in a scope that does not enclose the reference is not the binding it names, and the global stands. Both compilers agree on that much and then diverge downstream on the global itself: upstream emits `width:NaNpx`, where this compiler refuses the non-numeric identifier as a style value. That downstream divergence is what this entry is expected to read, and it is the same one `modules-1266-the-unshadowed-globals-in-a-style-value` records without any binding in the module -- so a regression in the binding question would change this entry's verdict while leaving that one's alone.

entries.label: the globals `NaN` and `Infinity` in a style value, bound nowhere
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the other half of the globals step
entries.note: With nothing bound, the step answers the global, which is what keeps this a divergence about the value rather than about the binding: upstream emits `width:NaNpx` and `height:Infinitypx`, where this compiler refuses a non-numeric identifier as a style value. Unchanged by the globals step and recorded so that it stays unchanged -- a regression that made the step refuse an unbound global would show up here as a message change rather than silently.

entries.label: a style value reading the name a string-named import specifier was aliased away from
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the imported-name fallback in the import lookup
entries.note: `import { "spacing" as sp }` binds `sp` and leaves `spacing` naming nothing, so upstream refuses -- it asks the scope for the binding a reference resolves to and never sees an aliased-away name. This compiler matched the specifier by its imported name, then re-searched the declaration by the local one and aborted with `Could not resolve the import specifier.` Both refuse once the fallback is deleted.

entries.label: a member read off a theme import whose export name is a string
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: The lookup half of the question. A string-named specifier binds only `c`, and the string is the export name the variable is hashed from -- so the class name and the `var()` it names have to be the ones the export name produces, not the ones the local alias would. Both compilers write `--x38wx3q`.

entries.label: a theme import whose export name is a string, read with no member access
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: The emit half. The group itself carries no value form, and this row is where it is read by the one name the import actually binds -- the sibling row reading the aliased-away name asks about the lookup instead. It compiled to nothing here until the object evaluator stopped answering a theme reference with "no value"; both refuse now, with the reference implementation's sentence.

entries.label: a theme import whose export name is the empty string
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: The shortest export name the grammar allows, and the one a name-keyed lookup is likeliest to read as absent. Hashed as a name of zero length on both sides.

entries.label: a theme import whose export name is the string `default`
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: `import { "default" as d }` names the default export through a named specifier, so the step that refuses a default import never sees it -- on either side. Both resolve it as the export named `default` and hash that name. Recorded because the refusal a reader would expect from the default-import step is the one neither compiler gives.

entries.label: a theme import whose export name carries a lone surrogate
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: An export name that is well-formed UTF-16 and not well-formed Unicode -- the one string an export name can hold that has no encoding a hash can read. Both refuse; upstream refuses it in the parser and this compiler where the name is decoded, so the sentences differ and the outcome does not.

entries.label: a theme import whose export name is a single astral character
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: One code point, two UTF-16 code units, four UTF-8 bytes -- the boundary where a hash fed code units and a hash fed code points part company. Both write `--xardzau`, so neither does.

entries.label: a theme import whose export name is a thousand characters long
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: The length boundary. The export name is hashed whole, so a truncating or fixed-buffer read would show here and nowhere else; both write `--xy7n7vi`.

entries.label: one string export name bound twice under two local names
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: Two bindings of one export name. The variable is the export name's, so both reads have to write the same `var()` through different locals -- which is the check that the alias contributes nothing to the hash.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a theme import whose export name is a string
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: Issue #1266's shape spelled through a string-named specifier: the parameter takes the local name over while the static read beside it still resolves the import. The parameter wins on both sides, so one rule reads the theme variable and the other the inline custom property.

entries.label: a member off a string-named theme import read eight condition levels deep
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: Depth does not change what the name resolves to, and this row is the measurement rather than the claim. Its pseudo-classes nest alphabetically on purpose: nested out of that order they hash a different selector on the two sides for a reason that has nothing to do with resolution, which `modules-three-nested-pseudo-classes-hash-differently` owns.

entries.label: a function-map entry imported under a string export name and called
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the string-named specifier read by its own local binding
entries.note: The injected function map is keyed by the name a reference spells, and a string-named specifier is how that name comes to differ from the export it binds. Called through its local alias the specifier still folds to `keyframes` on both sides.

entries.label: a style value reading the name an identifier-aliased import specifier was aliased away from
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the imported-name fallback in the import lookup
entries.note: The identifier spelling of the entry above. It refused on both compilers before the fallback was deleted too -- an imported identifier carries the syntax context the parser gave it and a reference carries the resolver's, so the two never compared equal. Recorded beside the string spelling because only the pair shows that the answer is the same for both.

entries.label: a constant declared under the name an import was aliased away from
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, what the imported-name fallback cost
entries.note: The name is free for the module to declare, and the declaration is what the reference resolves to on both compilers. The import lookup used to answer for the aliased-away name first, so the declaration was never read and the module aborted. Both references are in one style object so the alias's own binding is measured beside it: `sp.small` still resolves to the theme it names.

entries.label: a createTheme second argument named after an import's aliased-away name
entries.origin: code review of the imported-name fallback deletion, the second consumer of the import lookup
entries.note: The evaluator is not the only reader of the import lookup: `createTheme`'s second-argument check asks it whether an identifier is an import. Deleting the imported-name fallback changes which arm answers here -- the reference was refused as an import before and is refused as an unbound, non-static value now -- so the message changes while the verdict does not. Recorded because a message change is invisible to the harness, and the entry is what says the verdict was measured rather than assumed.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing the stylex namespace import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the reference implementation's own scope-blindness
entries.note: `functions.identifiers` is keyed by name and consulted ahead of any binding, on both compilers and deliberately -- an arrow parameter is injected into that same map. So `stylex` in the body is the map registered for the namespace import, `{ when }`, and not the parameter, and namespace validation refuses `when` as a key that is neither a pseudo nor an at-rule nor `default`. Both refuse; this compiler used to refuse at the style-value consumer with a sentence about a static expression, because the map carried no expression form. The exact text is asserted in `validation_stylex_create_test::invalid_values`, which is where a message can be pinned -- `both-reject` compares acceptance, not wording.

entries.label: a shadowed namespace parameter beside a static property
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the shape that reaches the consumer with something already collected
entries.note: The refusal belongs to the value, not to the namespace, so a property already folded beside it does not spare it. Kept apart from the entry above because the consumer is reached with a non-empty accumulator here.

entries.label: a shadowed namespace parameter read under a condition, inside a pseudo, and in a shorthand
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the value walk and the shorthand expansion
entries.note: The value walk recurses per condition key and a shorthand is carried into synthesized longhands, so a materialization that only happened at the top level would leave these three on the old message. Three shapes in one module because none can pass while another fails -- they share the one consumer.

entries.label: `when` read as a callee off a shadowed namespace parameter
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the guard the materialization is written to keep
entries.note: A guard, and the reason the map is materialized at the style-value consumer rather than where the identifier resolves: `when` is read off the map as a callee, which needs the map's own form. Materializing at the identifier seam would compile this to nothing.

entries.label: `when` read as a callee off the namespace import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the same callee without a parameter in the way
entries.note: The other half of the guard above. The reference does not go through a parameter, so a regression that broke the map's own form would report here even with no shadowing case in the corpus.

entries.label: `when` read as a callee off a bare named import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the bare spelling of the callee guard
entries.note: `when` imported on its own is a separate registration from the key on the namespace map, so it is a separate guard.

entries.label: a parameter shadowing the namespace import and never read
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the control on the fold
entries.note: A guard. The fold happens where the name is read, not where it is bound, so this compiles on both compilers. A materialization that fired on the parameter list would refuse it.

entries.label: a shadowed namespace parameter inside an array style value
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the fold reached through an array
entries.note: Upstream reads `A style array value can only contain strings or numbers.`; this compiler still reads `Style value must evaluate to a static expression.` -- not because of the fold but because every array written inside a dynamic style's body aborts at the same consumer, folded map or not. Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/14-an-array-style-value-inside-a-dynamic-style.md`. `both-reject` cannot report the wording, so this row holds the input rather than measuring the message.

entries.label: the stylex namespace import read as a static style value
entries.source:
import * as stylex from '@stylexjs/stylex';

export const styles = stylex.create({ a: { height: stylex } });
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the same fold at the static consumer
entries.note: No shadowing: the namespace import itself, read where a value belongs. A static namespace is evaluated by `nodes/object_expression.rs`, which deopts rather than materializing, so this reads `A style value can only contain an array, string or number.` where upstream reads `Invalid pseudo or at-rule.` Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/15-the-function-map-read-where-it-is-not-a-map.md`.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named import that is a function-map entry
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the function-map entries that are not maps
entries.note: Upstream folds `{ fn: keyframes }` and refuses it as a namespace, and this compiler now folds the same object and refuses on the same key `fn`. It used to register `keyframes` as a config the identifier step had no value form for and deopted -- and a deopt inside a dynamic style is the inline-style path, so this emitted `height:var(--x-height)` for a module upstream refuses. The keyframes call is here because this row was written while a shadowing parameter as the specifier's only occurrence still lost the specifier to type stripping; that is fixed for a JavaScript input and `modules-1266-param-shadows-a-named-import-referenced-nowhere-else` now measures the bare shape. The call stays: it is the shape where the entry is also read as a callee, which is why the fold is built at the style-value consumer rather than where the identifier resolves. `both-reject` cannot report the wording, which is pinned in `validation_stylex_create_test::invalid_values`. Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/16-a-shadowed-function-import-emits-css-upstream-refuses.md`.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named `firstThatWorks` import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the second entry of the `{ fn }` family
entries.note: The same fold as `modules-1266-param-shadows-a-named-function-map-import` through a different entry shape -- an array-args config rather than an expression one -- so it is the guard that the fold is a property of a function config and not of one registration. The other create call keeps the specifier alive.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a bare `when` import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the entry whose keys are not `fn`
entries.note: The one entry of the family upstream registers as the marker object itself rather than as `{ fn }`, so the object the parameter folds to carries the marker names and `ancestor` is the key the refusal lands on. Same sentence either way. The other create call both keeps the specifier alive and guards `when` as a callee, which is why the fold is built at the style-value consumer and not where the identifier resolves.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named `positionTry` import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the third entry of the `{ fn }` family
entries.note: Found by reading the registration rather than by report: `positionTry` is registered exactly as `keyframes` is, so it diverged exactly as `keyframes` did and is fixed by the same fold.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named import that nothing else reads
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the shape the fold cannot reach
entries.note: The reported shape. It used to be divergent for a reason that was not the fold: the type-stripping pass ran ahead of the transform and elided a specifier with no value reference, and a shadowing parameter is not a reference, so `keyframes` was gone before anything could register it. Eliding it is TypeScript's rule and this subject is a `.js` file, so the pass now keeps every specifier of a JavaScript input and the fold sees the name. A TypeScript input keeps the elision and still compiles -- a decided divergence this corpus cannot ask, because every subject is handed the same filename; it is pinned in `__test__/importElision.spec.ts` instead. Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/22-the-stripped-specifier-the-fold-never-sees.md`.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named `defaultMarker` import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the entry that is a function and not an object
entries.note: The one entry of the family upstream registers as a function, so it refuses with `A style value can only contain an array, string or number.` rather than as a namespace. Here the entry is an index map with no value form and the build stops on a sentence about that shape instead. Reaching upstream's sentence needs the namespace validator to refuse a value it currently passes over, which is wider than this seam. Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/21-a-shadowed-default-marker-param-reports-an-internal-shape.md`.

entries.label: a named `keyframes` import read as a static style value
entries.source:
import { create, keyframes } from '@stylexjs/stylex';

export const styles = create({ a: { height: keyframes } });
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the same fold at the static consumer
entries.note: No shadowing: the import itself, read where a value belongs. The static object evaluator deopts rather than materializing, so this reads `A style value can only contain an array, string or number.` where upstream reads `Invalid pseudo or at-rule.` -- the same divergence `modules-1266-the-namespace-import-read-as-a-static-value` holds, now reached through a function config too. It used to read `Function not found`, which named nothing a caller could act on. Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/15-the-function-map-read-where-it-is-not-a-map.md`.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a named `types` import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the one function-map name that agrees
entries.note: A guard, and the one name of the family that agrees on purpose: upstream never registers `types` for a create call, so nothing folds and the parameter stands. This compiler does not register it for a create call either -- only for `defineVars` and `createTheme` -- so now that the entries beside it fold and refuse, this one agrees for the reason upstream does rather than because a deopt happened to land in the same place.

entries.label: a shadowed namespace parameter coerced to a string in a template
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the fold read where a string is expected
entries.note: Both compilers emit nonsense and disagree about which: upstream gives `height:[object Object]px`, which is what JS gives for an object in a template, and this compiler coerces the fold to the empty string and gives `height:px`. Recorded rather than fixed -- agreeing here means reproducing a coercion neither compiler intends. In `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/15-the-function-map-read-where-it-is-not-a-map.md`.

entries.label: a shadowed namespace parameter read as a computed key
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the same coercion in the key position
entries.note: Upstream coerces the fold and emits a rule for a property named `[object object]`; this compiler refuses the value. The key position of the entry above, kept apart because one accepts and one refuses and a single module could only report the refusal.

entries.label: a theme import read as a style value with no member access
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the shape the fall-through inventory missed
entries.note: The shape the row was filed for: it compiled to nothing here -- no rule, no error, no warning -- because the object evaluator answered a theme reference with `no value` and the caller read that as `no property`. Both compilers refuse it now, with the reference implementation's sentence. `both-reject` compares the outcome and not the text, so the wording is pinned in `validation_stylex_create_test::theme_reference_style_values`.

entries.label: a dropped theme object beside a property that does emit
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the drop made visible
entries.note: The same value with a sibling that survives, which is why the drop read as a compiling module rather than as a bug: the `color` rule was emitted alone and the missing declaration looked like a style nobody had written. Both refuse now, and the sibling is refused with it.

entries.label: a dropped theme object under a condition and in a shorthand
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the drop through the value walk
entries.note: The value is read per condition key and through synthesized longhands alike, so neither depth nor shorthand expansion changes the answer -- it was the same drop in both, and it is the same refusal in both. Recorded together because they share the one arm.

entries.label: a theme import coerced to a string in a style value
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the one row upstream emits on
entries.note: The one shape in this family where the reference implementation emits rather than refuses: it coerces the group through its own `toString` and ships `z-index:x1q8i56t` -- the var-group hash as a z-index, meaningless CSS that hashes a class name all the same. Measured and deliberately not mirrored: an interpolation with no string form contributes nothing here, and the seam is the template evaluator rather than the style-value arm -- it drops every such interpolation, not only a theme reference. Filed as issue 23 of this effort.

entries.label: a namespace theme import read as a style value
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the namespace spelling of the drop
entries.note: The namespace spelling, kept apart from the named one because the two refusals were not the same sentence: upstream cannot resolve a namespace import of a theme file at all (`Referenced constant is not defined.`) where this compiler resolved it and then refused the group as a value. The resolution member reads relied on turned out to hash the local alias rather than an export, so it went -- see `modules-1266-a-namespace-theme-import` -- and this now reads upstream's sentence for upstream's reason.

entries.label: a member read off a namespace import of a theme file
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the namespace arm of the resolution chain
entries.note: A namespace specifier binds the whole export object, so it names no export a theme reference could be built from -- which is why upstream excludes it from the import step and lets it fall through to `Referenced constant is not defined.` This compiler synthesized the *local alias* as the export name instead, so `tokens.color` folded to a variable hashed from `vars.stylex.js//tokens.color` while the file's `defineVars` group exports `vars` and defines `vars.stylex.js//vars.color`. Both hashes were measured against the reference implementation's own output for the theme file; only an alias spelled the same as the exported group ever agreed. `acceptance divergent` before the arm lands, and a `var()` nothing defines after it, which renders as nothing and reports as nothing.

entries.label: a namespace theme import read through the group it exports
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the spelling the namespace form actually calls for
entries.note: The spelling an author reaching for a namespace import would write: the exported group, then the variable. It diverged before the arm landed too, and in the same direction -- the alias-hashed theme reference answered a string for `.vars`, and the second member hop read into that string -- so the correct spelling was refused while the incorrect one silently emitted a dangling variable. Kept apart from the entry above because it is the shape that shows the old resolution was not what the author meant either.

entries.label: one token read through a namespace import and through a named one at once
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the shape that shows the two resolutions disagreeing
entries.note: The same variable of the same theme file, named twice in one module. Before the namespace arm landed this emitted two different custom properties -- the named half the one the theme file defines, the namespace half a hash of the local alias -- so the divergence was visible without leaving the module or reading the theme file. Both compilers refuse the module now, on the namespace half.

entries.label: a namespace theme import whose alias is spelled like the exported group
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the one namespace spelling that used to agree with the theme file
entries.note: The coincidence the old resolution rested on: hashing the local alias is right exactly when the alias is spelled like the exported group, and this is that case. It was the only namespace shape whose `var()` the theme file actually defines, and upstream refused it all the same. Recorded so the decision to refuse is read as giving up a coincidence rather than a capability -- the same variable is reachable by the named import the reference implementation and this compiler both resolve.

entries.label: a member read off a namespace import of a file that is not a theme file
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the namespace arm reached without a theme file behind it
entries.note: Nothing about the refusal is specific to a theme file, and the specifier is answered before any path is resolved. This read as `Could not resolve the path to the imported file.` before -- the wrong reason for the right refusal, and the same wrong reason the default-import case read before its own step landed. Both refuse either way, so the entry guards the reason rather than the verdict; the sentence is pinned in `validation_stylex_create_test::invalid_values`.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter shadowing a namespace theme import
entries.origin: the identifier audit for issue #1266, the shadowing half of the namespace arm
entries.note: The namespace arm of the import lookup already compared the binding rather than the name, so this half was never broken -- and with the import no longer resolving anything, the parameter is the only reference to the name and compiles to an inline style on both compilers. Recorded so that a regression to a name match reports here: it would resolve the parameter to the import and refuse the module instead.

entries.label: a theme import read as a style value inside a dynamic style
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the same shape at the dynamic consumer
entries.note: The other consumer of a style value: it refused where the static one dropped, but with a sentence about a static expression rather than about the value. Both consumers read the reference implementation's sentence now, so this row holds the outcome and the wording is pinned in `validation_stylex_create_test::theme_reference_style_values`.

entries.label: a theme member read beside a dynamic parameter
entries.origin: code review of the folded-map consumer, the control on the drop
entries.note: A guard, and the reason the family went unnoticed: with the member access the reference resolves to a theme reference, folds to a `var()` and agrees exactly. A fix that started refusing theme references outright would pass every row above and fail here.

entries.label: three pseudo-classes nested in an order that is not alphabetical
entries.origin: the depth boundary written for issue #1266, which surfaced it
entries.note: The leaf selector is `:focus:hover:active` here and `:active:focus:hover` upstream, so the two hash different class names for one authored style. Upstream sorts the whole accumulated pseudo-class list; this compiler sorts each pair as it nests and appends the third, which is why two of them agree in either nesting order and three agree only when the nesting order is already alphabetical. Nothing to do with reference resolution -- it was found by the guard written for it, `modules-1266-a-shadowed-param-at-extreme-condition-depth`, which nests its pseudo-classes alphabetically so this divergence is measured once, here. Owned by `.scratch/fix_dynamic-param-shadows-import/issues/19-three-nested-pseudo-classes-hash-differently.md`.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter beside a static prop that reads nothing
entries.origin: issue #1266, the second shape that compiled before the fix
entries.note: The other half of the pair recorded as `modules-1266-import-unreferenced-elsewhere`: a static prop stands beside the dynamic style but reads no imported name. The import used to be elided here too, so the name match had nothing to match; a `.js` subject now keeps it and the match runs against a declaration that is present. Held by the binding comparison, which is the only thing left holding it.

entries.label: a dynamic parameter named `firstThatWorks`, which nothing imports under that name
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the name-keyed function map
entries.note: `functions.identifiers` is name-keyed and consulted before the chain, but it holds a name only where that name was imported: this module imports the namespace, so nothing is registered under `firstThatWorks` and the parameter has to stay an ordinary parameter. The shape where the name *is* imported is `modules-1266-param-shadows-a-named-function-map-import`, which diverges; keying the map on a fixed list of API names rather than on what the module imports would collapse the two and show here.

entries.label: a style value reading a name bound to a function declaration
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the last step of the chain
entries.note: A hoisted binding with no declarator: it reaches the end of the chain and is refused for its declaration kind. It is also the case the early-declaration step must not answer for -- a function holds its value from the top of its scope, so a reference above one is not early -- and the step before it must not answer for either, since the declaration lookup asks for a `VarDeclarator` and finds none. Both compilers refuse with the sentence `Unsupported expression: FunctionDeclaration`.

entries.label: a style value reading a name bound to a class declaration
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the last step of the chain
entries.note: The sibling of the function-declaration refusal, and recorded apart from it because the two are separate declaration lists consulted in one call: a fix that dropped either list would leave the other passing. Both compilers refuse with the sentence `Unsupported expression: ClassDeclaration`.

entries.label: a member of a `const` mutated in place, then read as a style value
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the mutated-binding step
entries.note: The binding is never rebound, so only the mutation set can refuse it. Splitting one write set into a reassignment set and a mutation set was meant to change no outcome; this is the row that says the mutation half is still filled. Both compilers refuse with the sentence `Referenced value is not a constant.`

entries.label: a `const` array mutated through a method call, then read as a style value
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the mutated-binding step
entries.note: Mutation through a method receiver rather than through an assignment, which the same walk records. A length read is the value because it folds on both compilers when the binding is left alone, so what the verdict measures is the refusal and not the read.

entries.label: a `const` passed as an `Object.assign` target, then read as a style value
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the mutated-binding step
entries.note: The third producer the mutation walk records, and the one that reaches the binding through an argument position rather than through a member expression.

entries.label: a `let` reassigned after its declaration, then read as a style value
entries.origin: issue #1266, the guard on the reassigned-binding step
entries.note: The other half of the split write set. Both halves refuse with the same text, so the split is only observable as this row and the mutation rows above continuing to refuse independently.

entries.label: a `const` object neither rebound nor mutated, read as a style value
entries.origin: issue #1266, the control on the two write steps
entries.note: The control the refusal rows need: the same module with the write removed has to fold. A step that probed the declaration list rather than the write set would refuse every `const` and pass every row above.

entries.label: a value with an unclosed function, read through a binding
entries.origin: issue #1266, a malformed value reached through the chain rather than written inline
entries.note: What the chain answers is where a value came from, not whether it is CSS. Both compilers refuse with the sentence `Rule contains an unclosed function`, this one naming the repaired rule after it. One construct per row, because the first refusal ends the compile and a row carrying three would measure only the first.

entries.label: a value with an unclosed string, read through a binding
entries.origin: issue #1266, a malformed value reached through the chain rather than written inline
entries.note: The sibling refusal, and a different sentence: `Rule contains an unclosed string`. Kept apart from the unclosed function so each is measured rather than shadowed by whichever the compile reaches first.

entries.label: a value with an unclosed bracket, read through a binding
entries.origin: issue #1266, the malformed value neither compiler refuses
entries.note: The third construct, and the one that is not refused at all: both compilers emit `grid-template-columns:[full-start 1fr` verbatim and hash the same class from it. Worth a row of its own precisely because it agrees -- an unclosed bracket is not repaired the way an unclosed function and string are, so a chain change that started refusing it would show here as an acceptance divergence rather than nowhere.

entries.label: a custom property written from a shadowed parameter and from a binding
entries.origin: issue #1266, the custom-property path through the chain
entries.note: A custom property is not expanded or validated the way a known property is, so it reaches the value walk by a different path: the static read has to keep its theme reference and the shadowed parameter has to become an inline variable, in the one module where both are spelled on the same key.

entries.label: a vendor-prefixed property written from a shadowed parameter
entries.origin: issue #1266, the prefixed-property path through the chain
entries.note: Neither compiler adds a vendor prefix, so the prefix has to be authored to be measured: `WebkitLineClamp` is normalized to `-webkit-line-clamp` and takes two different folded values for one property, a theme reference on the static prop and an inline variable on the dynamic one. Both declarations are emitted prefixed on both sides, which is what makes this a measurement rather than agreement about nothing.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter read eight condition levels deep
entries.origin: issue #1266, the depth boundary on the recursive value walk
entries.note: `modules-1266-nested-conditions` asks the same question three levels down; this asks it at eight, interleaving at-rules with pseudo-classes, where the condition key list is longer than any authored style is likely to be. The walk is recursive on both compilers, so what a depth this size measures is that neither runs out of anything before the leaf. The pseudo-classes are nested in alphabetical order deliberately: any other nesting order makes the selector-order divergence recorded as `modules-three-nested-pseudo-classes-hash-differently` decide this row's verdict instead of the resolution this row is a guard on, and restoring one here is a step of the ticket that owns it.

entries.label: twelve dynamic styles in one create, each shadowing a different import
entries.source:
import * as stylex from '@stylexjs/stylex';
import { a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, k, l } from 'tokens.stylex.js';

export const styles = stylex.create({
  wrapper: {
    marginTop: a.x,
    marginBottom: b.x,
    marginInlineStart: c.x,
    marginInlineEnd: d.x,
    paddingTop: e.x,
    paddingBottom: f.x,
    paddingInlineStart: g.x,
    paddingInlineEnd: h.x,
    borderTopWidth: i.x,
    borderBottomWidth: j.x,
    rowGap: k.x,
    columnGap: l.x,
  },
  dynA: (a) => ({ marginTop: a }),
  dynB: (b) => ({ marginBottom: b }),
  dynC: (c) => ({ marginInlineStart: c }),
  dynD: (d) => ({ marginInlineEnd: d }),
  dynE: (e) => ({ paddingTop: e }),
  dynF: (f) => ({ paddingBottom: f }),
  dynG: (g) => ({ paddingInlineStart: g }),
  dynH: (h) => ({ paddingInlineEnd: h }),
  dynI: (i) => ({ borderTopWidth: i }),
  dynJ: (j) => ({ borderBottomWidth: j }),
  dynK: (k) => ({ rowGap: k }),
  dynL: (l) => ({ columnGap: l }),
});
entries.origin: issue #1266, the breadth boundary on one create call
entries.note: Every name in the module is both an import and a parameter, so each of the twenty-four reads is decided only by which binding it carries. One evaluation cache is shared across the call, and a cache keyed on the symbol alone rather than on the symbol and its syntax context would answer the second read of a name with the first one's value -- which is the failure this breadth, and not depth, is written to catch.

entries.label: a shadowed dynamic parameter spread into the style object
entries.origin: issue #1266, the parameter in the one position that is not a value
entries.note: A spread asks the evaluator to enumerate the parameter's keys rather than to fold it to a value, which is the position with no inline-style fall-through to deopt into. Recorded because the abort this effort fixed came from a resolved value having no expression form, and a spread is where that same value is asked for a shape instead. The two refusals are not the same sentence -- `Referenced constant is not defined.` here against `Only static values are allowed inside of a create() call.` upstream -- so this row holds the outcome and not the text.

entries.label: a theme import read inside a fallback array
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: Refused as an array rather than as a value, by both compilers, with the array-specific sentence. The neighbour that was already right, kept so the two cannot drift apart.

entries.label: a member read off a theme import as a style value
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: The guard the refusal needs: a member read is what a theme import is for, and it must keep resolving to the group's custom property. Records `identical` so a refusal that grew too wide reports as a changed verdict rather than as silence.

entries.label: a theme import read as a keyframes step value
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: A decided divergence. Upstream emits the step with the declaration missing and says nothing; here the value is refused, as every other shape with no value form in this position already is. The silent drop is what this effort removed, and keeping it for one call and not the others is what made it hard to see.

entries.label: a theme import read as a createTheme override value
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: A decided divergence, for the reason the keyframes step is. The group handed to `createTheme` as its first argument still resolves -- that is the position it belongs in.

entries.label: a theme import read as a positionTry fallback value
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: A decided divergence, for the reason the keyframes step is. Upstream emits `@position-try --x {}` -- the at-rule with nothing in it.

entries.label: a theme import read as a viewTransitionClass declaration value
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: A decided divergence, for the reason the keyframes step is. Upstream emits the part's selector with an empty body.

entries.label: a theme import read as a computed property key
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: A decided divergence. Upstream coerces the group to its hash and declares a property named after it -- `.x12l9qay{x1q8i56t:1px}`, which is not a property -- where this compiler refuses the key. Not a defect to reproduce.

entries.label: a theme import spread into a style object
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: A decided divergence. The object upstream folds the group to has no own enumerable properties, so the spread contributes nothing and the namespace compiles empty; here the spread refuses because the group's properties cannot be enumerated at compile time. The two answers agree about the CSS and disagree about whether saying so is worth stopping for.

entries.label: a theme import read as a defineConsts value
entries.origin: issue #1266, a theme reference read where a style value belongs
entries.note: The other declaring call that reads the same evaluator. Both refuse with the same sentence, and here for a reason of the position rather than of the value: a constant is inlined at its use sites, so nothing it holds may be a reference resolved later.
